title: The Gateway and the Envelope: Cerf, Kahn, and a Protocol for Networks That Cannot See Each Other
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Valley and the Rocket Engines

stops.name: New Haven, the birth
stops.date_confidence: Attested and invariant across every biography consulted, including the Internet Hall of Fame inductee page: 23 June 1943, New Haven, Connecticut. No source names the hospital or the ward, and none claims to.
stops.campa: Vinton Gray Cerf is born in New Haven, Connecticut, on the twenty-third of June, 1943. The city gives him a birth certificate and nothing further; the family moves west while he is small, and New Haven does not return in the record of his working life. Every biography carries the date without variance and none names the hospital. He will spend his working life on the joining of places that cannot see one another. This one never appears on his own map again.
suggested_refs: New Haven, Connecticut, birthplace named in every published biography and in no anecdote
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography of Vint Cerf

stops.name: Van Nuys High School, three boys in one building
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the three attended the same school: Wikipedia, 'Steve Crocker', states that Crocker attended Van Nuys High School, as did Vint Cerf and Jon Postel. The school year given here is a default within Cerf's high-school years; the coordinates are corrected to the campus at 6535 Cedros Avenue, the research pool's pair having fallen some 600 m northwest into residential blocks.
stops.campa: Cerf attends Van Nuys High School on Cedros Avenue in the same years as Steve Crocker and Jon Postel. Crocker will write the first Request for Comments; Postel will hold the assignment of the internet's numbers and names in his own hands for thirty years. All three will be at UCLA as graduate students within ten years, and in the same Network Working Group correspondence. Cerf is partly deaf from birth and has worn a hearing aid since he was thirteen, and he will marry a woman who is also deaf, met through the man who sells them their aids.
suggested_refs: Van Nuys High School, 6535 Cedros Avenue, attended by Cerf, Crocker, and Postel
sources: Internet Hall of Fame profiles of Cerf, Crocker, and Postel

stops.name: Canoga Park, six months on the F-1
stops.date_confidence: Attested in substance, reconstructed in place and date. Wikipedia reads: While in high school, Cerf worked at Rocketdyne on the Apollo program for six months, writing statistical-analysis software for F-1 engine tests. The research pool framed it as a pre-college job, which is wrong; 1961 is a vicinity and month and day are defaults. The pool gives only Los Angeles area for the location, so Rocketdyne's principal Canoga Park plant is used and flagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: While still in high school Cerf works six months at Rocketdyne, writing statistical analysis software for the test firings of the F-1, the engine that will lift the Saturn V off its pad. He is a boy reducing the numbers that come off a rocket motor being shaken to pieces in the hills above the Valley. Apollo is the largest engineering effort the country has, and his part in it is arithmetic performed by a machine at his instruction. The F-1 is the largest liquid-fuel engine anyone has built, and the numbers it throws off in testing are useless until somebody reduces them.
stops.quote: And programming computers was so fascinating. You create your own little universe, and then it does what you tell it to do.
stops.quote_source: Vint Cerf, interviewed by David Frank, AARP Bulletin, vol. 57 no. 10, December 2016, p. 28
suggested_refs: Rocketdyne's Canoga Park plant and the F-1 engine test program, 1961
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Stanford, the mathematics degree
stops.date_confidence: Attested year, defaulted month and day: Wikipedia gives a Bachelor of Science in mathematics from Stanford University in 1965. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Stanford pin, inherited unchanged from diffie.journey.json, hellman.journey.json, ralph_merkle.journey.json, and nick_szabo.journey.json.
stops.campa: Cerf takes a Bachelor of Science in mathematics and leaves Stanford in 1965. The campus is not yet the campus he will return to: the cryptographers who make this coordinate famous, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman and Ralph Merkle, are elsewhere and young, and the department that will employ him has not taken the shape it will take. He goes to work rather than straight into graduate school. The degree is in mathematics and not in engineering; the doctorate seven years later is the one in computers.
suggested_refs: Stanford University mathematics degree, 1965, on the atlas's canonical Stanford coordinate

stops.name: Los Angeles, IBM and QUIKTRAN
stops.date_confidence: Attested employment, reconstructed address. Wikipedia and the Internet Hall of Fame have Cerf working about two years as an IBM systems engineer supporting QUIKTRAN after Stanford. The research pool concedes the exact building is not confirmed in public sources; the pair used is the downtown Los Angeles centroid and stands for the city, not for an IBM door. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: For about two years Cerf is a systems engineer at IBM in Los Angeles, supporting QUIKTRAN, a time sharing system that lets many users at terminals share one mainframe between them. It is ordinary corporate computing, and nothing in it resembles a network. The job keeps him inside machines long enough to want to go back to school for them. QUIKTRAN is a system many people use at once and none of them owns. Which building IBM assigned him to is not recorded anywhere consulted.
stops.quote: You literally walked inside the computer, a room with glowing red tubes on the walls. It was weird, but I was mesmerized.
stops.quote_source: Vint Cerf, quoted in Tekla S. Perry, 'Meet Mr. Internet: Vint Cerf,' IEEE Spectrum, 30 April 2023
suggested_refs: IBM's QUIKTRAN time-sharing service, supported by Cerf 1965 to 1967
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Boelter Hall 3420, the first node
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: the UCLA Computer Science Department history, Leonard Kleinrock's published accounts, and the markers at Boelter Hall date the installation of the first Interface Message Processor in room 3420 to 2 September 1969. Cerf's membership of Kleinrock's group and of the Network Measurement Center is attested from 1967 by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Cerf comes back to graduate school in 1967, into Leonard Kleinrock's group at UCLA, and on the second of September 1969 an Interface Message Processor is wheeled into room 3420 of Boelter Hall and wired to Kleinrock's host computer. It is the first node of the ARPANET, and for some weeks it is the whole of it, a network with one member. Cerf works in the Network Measurement Center, gathering the statistics that tell the young network whether it is working at all. The room is preserved and marked.
suggested_refs: Boelter Hall room 3420, UCLA, preserved as the ARPANET's first node

stops.name: UCLA, RFC 20 and the common alphabet
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day from the document itself: RFC 20, 'ASCII format for Network Interchange,' V. Cerf, UCLA, 16 October 1969, read directly.
stops.campa: Six weeks after the machine arrives Cerf writes RFC 20, a few pages fixing the ASCII character set as the alphabet in which machines on this network will address each other. It is not a famous document and it does the least glamorous kind of work: it says that a letter A shall be one particular number and no other, everywhere, without exception. Every protocol he writes afterward rests on an agreement of this kind, kept by several parties at once and worth nothing if one of them declines.
stops.quote: Deviations from the standard may create serious difficulties in information interchange and should be used only with full cognizance of the parties involved.
stops.quote_source: RFC 20, 'ASCII format for Network Interchange,' Vint Cerf, UCLA, 16 October 1969
suggested_refs: RFC 20, still the standing reference for ASCII in the RFC series

stops.name: SRI International, the second node
stops.date_confidence: Attested: SRI International's institutional history and standard ARPANET timelines date the first host-to-host message from UCLA to SRI to 29 October 1969, and place the Augmentation Research Center and the Network Information Center at the same site. Cerf's coordination with SRI on the Network Control Program is attested in general rather than by dated visit.
stops.campa: The second node stands at SRI in Menlo Park, in the institute that also holds Douglas Engelbart's Augmentation Research Center and the Network Information Center that will catalogue the growing net. On the twenty-ninth of October the first message is sent from Boelter Hall to this machine and the system fails after two letters. Cerf coordinates with SRI as the Network Control Program takes shape, the modest protocol that TCP will later replace. From this date the network has more than one place to call.
suggested_refs: SRI International, Menlo Park, second ARPANET node and home of the Network Information Center
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: University of Utah, the fourth node
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to Cerf. The Utah node and its place in Network Working Group correspondence are attested in the standard four-node histories (Hafner and Lyon among them), but no source consulted confirms Cerf's personal presence at Salt Lake City in this window. Month is the documented one, day is a default, and the pin stands for the correspondence rather than the man.
stops.campa: Utah is the fourth node, joined to Santa Barbara and Menlo Park and Los Angeles before the year ends, and the four machines make a network that can be drawn on one page. Cerf works its protocol questions from UCLA and belongs to the same Network Working Group correspondence the Utah men belong to. Whether he ever stood in the room at Salt Lake City is not recorded in anything consulted. The node is documented; the man at it is not. This pin is set for the correspondence rather than for a visit.
suggested_refs: The four-node ARPANET of December 1969: UCLA, SRI, Santa Barbara, Utah
sources: Hafner and Lyon, Where Wizards Stay Up Late

stops.name: UCLA, the doctorate
stops.date_confidence: Attested year and subject, defaulted month and day: Wikipedia gives the master's degree in 1970 and the PhD in 1972, with the dissertation 'Multiprocessors, Semaphores, and a Graph Model of Computation' under Gerald Estrin.
stops.campa: Cerf takes his master's in 1970 and his doctorate in 1972 under Gerald Estrin, with a dissertation on multiprocessors, semaphores, and a graph model of computation: a study of how separate processes that cannot see one another are kept from trampling each other's work. He is writing about coordination between things that do not share a memory. Two years later he will publish the same problem restated at the scale of continents, and the answer will have the same shape as this one.
suggested_refs: Cerf's UCLA dissertation, 'Multiprocessors, Semaphores, and a Graph Model of Computation,' 1972

stops.name: Stanford, the assistant professorship
stops.date_confidence: Attested tenure, defaulted month and day: Stanford faculty records and Wikipedia give Cerf as assistant professor of computer science and electrical engineering from 1972 to 1976. Diffie's and Hellman's presence on this campus in the same years is attested in diffie.journey.json, whose Stanford pin this stop inherits byte for byte.
stops.campa: Cerf returns to Stanford as an assistant professor and teaches one of the first courses anywhere in internetworking. Robert Kahn brings him the problem directly from DARPA: make packet radio nets, satellite nets, and the ARPANET speak to one another without any of them being rebuilt or even told what the others are. On this same campus, in these same years, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman work toward the paper that opens public key cryptography, and Ralph Merkle crosses the bay with a manuscript a referee has rejected.
stops.quote: The networks couldn't be changed and couldn't know that they were part of the Internet, because they already existed.
stops.quote_source: Vint Cerf, quoted in Tekla S. Perry, 'Meet Mr. Internet: Vint Cerf,' IEEE Spectrum, 30 April 2023
suggested_refs: Stanford's first internetworking seminar, taught while the protocol was being designed

stops.name: University of Sussex, the international working group
stops.date_confidence: Attested month and place from Cerf's own retrospective accounts (ACM oral history, Internet Hall of Fame interview) and International Network Working Group meeting records for September 1973; the day is a default. The quote is from the paper published the following May, not from the meeting itself.
stops.campa: In September Cerf carries the problem to Falmer, outside Brighton, and lays it before the International Network Working Group: an audience of Europeans and Americans who each have a network of their own and no way to reach the others. He argues for gateways, machines standing between networks and translating, rather than for one network that swallows all the rest. The design work follows in California. The meeting is where the shape of it is first said aloud to people who are not already convinced.
stops.quote: Even though many different and complex problems must be solved in the design of an individual packet switching network, these problems are manifestly compounded when dissimilar networks are interconnected.
stops.quote_source: Cerf and Kahn, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication,' IEEE Transactions on Communications COM-22 no. 5, May 1974 (published after this meeting)
suggested_refs: International Network Working Group meeting, University of Sussex, September 1973

stops.name: Palo Alto, the sketch on hotel paper
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The anecdote of a diagram drawn on hotel paper in 1973 is widely repeated and Cerf has himself described sketching the architecture on the back of an envelope in a hotel lobby, but sources differ on the hotel, the month, and the medium, and no primary document naming the building was found. The research pool's own two lenses disagree on the coordinate: geography and afterlife both give 37.4419, -122.143 while naming a Hyatt on El Camino Real, whose properties lie about 4 km southeast. The El Camino strip pair is used and the disagreement is left standing.
stops.campa: Through the autumn Cerf and Kahn work out the layered design in Bay Area hotels between meetings, and the story that survives is of three rectangles drawn on hotel paper: host, gateway, destination network. Cerf has told it himself, of an envelope in a lobby. The accounts differ on the hotel, on the month, and on whether the paper was a napkin or stationery, and no primary document names the building. What is not in doubt is the content of the drawing, which is published the following May.
stops.quote: We give a special name to this interface that performs these functions and call it a GATEWAY.
stops.quote_source: Cerf and Kahn, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication,' IEEE Transactions on Communications COM-22 no. 5, May 1974
suggested_refs: The Palo Alto hotel strip on El Camino Real, unlocated site of the 1973 sketch
sources: Cerf's own retrospective interviews and oral histories
Widely repeated origin anecdote in internet histories (varying by source)

stops.name: Stanford, the paper that names the gateway
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month from the publication itself: IEEE Transactions on Communications, vol. COM-22, no. 5, May 1974, fetched and read directly. The day is a default. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Stanford pin.
stops.campa: In May the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers publishes A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication by Vinton G. Cerf and Robert E. Kahn, describing a Transmission Control Program and the gateways between networks that neither network needs to understand. The paper does not describe a machine. It describes an agreement, and its whole ambition is that no existing network has to change anything about itself in order to join. The terms set out in it have not been renegotiated since.
stops.quote: A protocol that supports the sharing of resources that exist in different packet switching networks is presented.
stops.quote_source: Cerf and Kahn, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication,' IEEE Transactions on Communications COM-22 no. 5, May 1974, abstract
suggested_refs: The May 1974 IEEE paper, the founding document of TCP/IP
sources: Cerf and Kahn, IEEE Transactions on Communications COM-22 no. 5 (read directly)

stops.name: Stanford, RFC 675
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month from the document itself: RFC 675, 'Specification of Internet Transmission Control Program,' V. Cerf, Y. Dalal, C. Sunshine, December 1974, read directly. The day is a default.
stops.campa: In December Cerf, Yogen Dalal, and Carl Sunshine publish RFC 675, the first detailed specification of the Transmission Control Program, pages of state tables and sequence numbers. Its acknowledgments credit Ray Tomlinson with the three way handshake and with initial sequence number selection, and thank Postel, Kahn, Burchfiel, Plummer and others by name. The document is written to be argued with by anyone who reads it, and it says as much at its own end.
stops.quote: Of course, we remain responsible for the remaining errors and misstatements which no doubt lurk in the nooks and crannies of the text.
stops.quote_source: RFC 675, 'Specification of Internet Transmission Control Program,' Cerf, Dalal and Sunshine, December 1974
suggested_refs: RFC 675, the first detailed TCP specification

stops.name: Arlington, the program manager's office
stops.date_confidence: Attested and corrected. The Internet Hall of Fame gives Cerf's DARPA tenure as 1976 to 1982; Stanford records and Wikipedia have him a Stanford professor 1972 to 1976. The research pool's chronology claimed a move in 1973, which is wrong by three years and contradicts its own other entries; the error descends from Wikipedia's loose phrase that Cerf worked at DARPA from 1973, which describes DARPA-funded work begun at Stanford. Month and day are defaults, and the coordinate is corrected to 1400 Wilson Boulevard, the agency's address through his tenure.
stops.campa: Cerf leaves Stanford in 1976 for the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency on Wilson Boulevard and becomes program manager of the Internetting project under Kahn. From this office he funds packet radio, packet satellite, network security, and the protocol itself across a scattered set of universities and contractors, holding a research program together by memorandum and telephone. Accounts often date the move to 1973; the agency's own record of his tenure begins in 1976, and the earlier date describes money, not employment.
suggested_refs: DARPA at 1400 Wilson Boulevard, Arlington, seat of the Internetting program
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: The Bayshore Freeway, the van with a radio
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day in DARPA and internet-history accounts of the three-network demonstration of 22 November 1977 and in Cerf's own retrospectives. The coordinate is a point on US 101 near Menlo Park and stands for a moving vehicle, which no pin can properly hold.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of November a van fitted with a packet radio set drives the Bayshore Freeway near Menlo Park while data leaves it, crosses a radio net, an ARPANET gateway, and a satellite hop to Europe, and comes back, without ever needing to know which network it was on. Three separate networks behave as one. It is the demonstration of what the 1974 paper claimed, run on a public highway at ordinary traffic speed, with Cerf overseeing the experiment.
suggested_refs: The packet radio van on US 101, 22 November 1977, first working internetwork
sources: DARPA and internet-history accounts of the November 1977 demonstration

stops.name: University College London, the far leg
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Peter Kirstein's published accounts of UCL's early ARPANET and SATNET connectivity, and internet-history records of the 22 November 1977 demonstration, place UCL as the far end of the three-network path.
stops.campa: The packets from the California van reach Peter Kirstein's group at University College London, are turned around, and go back the way they came. Kirstein's laboratory has been the ARPANET's earliest overseas partner since the start of the decade, connected while the whole network still ran to a few dozen hosts. The path holds across an ocean and a continent as it holds across a corridor. The network is now in two countries at once, and it stays that way.
suggested_refs: Peter Kirstein's group at University College London, the ARPANET's first foreign partner
sources: Internet-history records of the 1977 three-network test

stops.name: Kjeller, the satellite leg and its disputed ground station
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a correction to the research pool, which named Kjeller as the satellite ground station of the 1977 test and tagged it attested. Wikipedia's 'Internet protocol suite' routes the demonstration via England, Boston and Sweden; NORSAR's own article records it as the first non-US ARPANET site, joined June 1973 by way of the Tanum earth station in Sweden, and makes no mention of the November 1977 test. Coordinates for Kjeller are correct; the claim that the test passed through it is not.
stops.campa: NORSAR at Kjeller, the Norwegian seismic institute, is the first site outside the United States on the ARPANET, joined in June 1973 by satellite. The 1977 demonstration's satellite leg is usually told through Norway, but the documented route runs by way of the Tanum earth station in Sweden, and NORSAR's own record does not mention the November test at all. This pin stands for the northern edge of the network in these years, and the contradiction between the two tellings is left where it was found.
suggested_refs: NORSAR at Kjeller and the Tanum earth station in Sweden, the two Scandinavian claimants

stops.name: Cambridge, the working group at BBN
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to Cerf. BBN's role as builder of the Interface Message Processors and host of Network Working Group meetings is attested in the standard histories; no source consulted itemizes a particular day on which Cerf was in Cambridge. The date is a default within the DARPA years, and the coordinate is corrected to BBN's home at 10 Moulton Street, the research pool's pair having fallen 2 km east near Harvard.
stops.campa: Bolt Beranek and Newman on Moulton Street builds the Interface Message Processors and hosts a share of the Network Working Group meetings where protocol questions are settled line by line. Cerf, moving between Los Angeles, Stanford, and Arlington through the decade, belongs to this travelling seminar of engineers who meet wherever an institution has a room and a terminal. No source consulted itemizes a day on which he was in Cambridge, so the pin stands for the group and not for a visit.
suggested_refs: Bolt Beranek and Newman, 10 Moulton Street, builder of the ARPANET's IMPs
sources: Hafner and Lyon, Where Wizards Stay Up Late

stops.name: Arlington, Flag Day
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: DARPA and ARPANET records date the cutover from the Network Control Program to TCP/IP to 1 January 1983. No single ceremonial site is documented, and the research pool records that absence as a gap; the pin is the administrative center and stands for nobody's presence.
stops.campa: On the first of January 1983 the Network Control Program is switched off and TCP over IP becomes the only way anything on the ARPANET may speak. Hosts that have not converted simply stop being reachable. There is no ceremony and no room: the change happens on several hundred machines at once, coordinated by memoranda circulated for months beforehand. Cerf has spent ten years engineering toward this morning, and it passes without a photograph of anyone standing anywhere.
suggested_refs: The TCP/IP flag day of 1 January 1983, a transition with no ceremonial site
sources: DARPA and ARPANET historical records of the 1983 transition

stops.name: Washington, MCI and the mail
stops.date_confidence: Attested year and role: Wikipedia and MCI corporate history have Cerf leaving DARPA in 1982 for MCI as vice president of MCI Digital Information Services, leading the engineering of MCI Mail, which launched in 1983. Month and day are defaults and the coordinate is a Washington centroid rather than a confirmed office.
stops.campa: Cerf leaves government research for MCI as vice president of Digital Information Services and takes charge of engineering MCI Mail, which launches the following year. The work moves him out of protocol design and into product: billing, customer accounts, a paid service sold to a business world that does not yet believe electronic mail is worth money. He is arguing, from inside a telephone company, that the thing he helped build has a market and not only a research budget behind it.
suggested_refs: MCI Mail, engineered under Cerf and launched 1983
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Reston, back with Kahn at CNRI
stops.date_confidence: Attested year and role: CNRI institutional history and the Internet Hall of Fame have Cerf leaving MCI in 1986 to join Kahn's Corporation for National Research Initiatives as vice president. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Kahn has founded the Corporation for National Research Initiatives in Reston to keep internet research funded as DARPA's direct role recedes, and Cerf joins him there as vice president. The partnership that began in Bay Area hotels in 1973 now runs an institution of its own. Here he works on digital library systems, a line of work the Stanford Infobus will carry on from the other end of the decade under Nick Szabo's eye, and on the first groundwork of an interplanetary internet.
suggested_refs: The Corporation for National Research Initiatives, Reston, founded by Robert Kahn
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Washington, MCI Mail joins the internet
stops.date_confidence: Attested year: Wikipedia has MCI Mail becoming the first commercial email service connected to the Internet in 1989, under engineering Cerf had led. Month and day are defaults. The advocacy for privatization dated to 1988 is carried by the research pool at reconstruction, with no document cited.
stops.campa: MCI Mail becomes the first commercial electronic mail service connected to the internet, which means a paying customer of a telephone company can now write to a university and be answered. The wall between the research network and the commercial one is breached from the commercial side, by the man who wrote the research network's protocol. He has been arguing publicly since about 1988 for privatization; here the argument arrives as a product with a bill attached to it.
suggested_refs: MCI Mail's 1989 internet connection, the first commercial mail service on the net

stops.name: Reston, the Internet Society
stops.date_confidence: Attested year and role: the Internet Hall of Fame and Wikipedia have Cerf co-founding the Internet Society in 1992 and serving as its founding president. Month and day are defaults; the Reston coordinate stands for the corridor in which the organization and CNRI both sat.
stops.campa: Cerf co-founds the Internet Society and serves as its first president, an organization made to give the growing network a coordinating home belonging to no single government. The standards process moves under its roof, and the Internet Engineering Task Force acquires a legal body to sit inside. His work in this decade is organizational rather than technical. He is building institutions meant to outlast the protocols he wrote, on the argument that a network open by design does not stay open by itself.
suggested_refs: The Internet Society, founded 1992, later home of the IETF standards process
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Ashburn, the return to MCI
stops.date_confidence: Attested dates and title, reconstructed place. The Internet Hall of Fame reads: from 1994 to 2005, Cerf served as the senior vice president of Technology Strategy for MCI. The research pool's geography lens gave a different title, Internet architecture and technology, contradicting its own chronology; the sourced wording is used. The Ashburn pin stands for a tenure documented by title and dates, not by a confirmed address.
stops.campa: Cerf goes back to MCI as senior vice president of Technology Strategy and holds the post eleven years, through the company's absorption into WorldCom, the accounting collapse, and its re-emergence as MCI Incorporated. The office moves across the Washington region in that time and is not documented as a single address; Ashburn, in the data center corridor growing up around the network in these very years, stands for a tenure recorded by title and dates rather than by a door.
suggested_refs: Northern Virginia's data-center corridor, grown up around the network Cerf designed
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Washington, Gallaudet and the Bell Medal
stops.date_confidence: Attested year for both: Wikipedia has Cerf joining the Gallaudet University board of trustees in 1997 and receiving the IEEE Alexander Graham Bell Medal in the same year. Month and day are defaults; the coordinate is the Gallaudet campus in northeast Washington.
stops.campa: Cerf joins the board of trustees of Gallaudet University, the university for the deaf in northeast Washington, and in the same year the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers gives him its Alexander Graham Bell Medal. Bell spent a great part of his life arguing against exactly the kind of school Gallaudet is, insisting deaf children be taught to speak rather than to sign. Cerf, partly deaf since birth, takes the seat and takes the medal, and says nothing on the subject that any source consulted records.
suggested_refs: Gallaudet University, Washington, and the IEEE Alexander Graham Bell Medal, both 1997

stops.name: The White House, the National Medal of Technology
stops.date_confidence: Attested with an unresolved contradiction inside the research pool: its chronology lens dates the ceremony to December 1997, its geography lens to October 1997 and adds an East Room detail attested nowhere consulted. Wikipedia supports December, which is used, and the disagreement is recorded rather than settled. The citation is the official one; the widely quoted 'for founding and developing the Internet' is a paraphrase. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical White House pin, shared with bill_clinton.journey.json.
stops.campa: President Bill Clinton hands Cerf and Robert Kahn the National Medal of Technology, the country's highest honor for technological achievement. The official citation is nine words long: for creating and sustaining development of Internet Protocols. Twenty-three years separate the ceremony from the paper it is given for. The two men who agreed on a way for strangers' machines to exchange packets are received by a government that has, in the interval, come to depend on the agreement entirely.
suggested_refs: The 1997 National Medal of Technology citation, 'For creating and sustaining development of Internet Protocols'
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography
National Science and Technology Medals Foundation records

stops.name: Pasadena, the Interplanetary Internet
stops.date_confidence: Attested year: Wikipedia's 'Interplanetary Internet' has the JPL study started by a team led by Cerf and the late Adrian Hooke, with Cerf appointed a distinguished visiting scientist at JPL in 1998. Month and day are defaults. The coordinate is corrected to JPL itself, the research pool's afterlife lens having pinned a point 2 km south in Pasadena proper.
stops.campa: Cerf is made a distinguished visiting scientist at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and, with Adrian Hooke, begins the study of an interplanetary internet: a network for distances at which light itself is slow and a link may be gone for hours because a planet is in the way. The answer is delay tolerant networking, in which a message is held and forwarded rather than dropped when the far end cannot be reached. It is the layering argument of 1974, carried out to where the ocean is vacuum.
suggested_refs: The Jet Propulsion Laboratory's Interplanetary Internet study, begun 1998

stops.name: Marina del Rey, the ICANN board
stops.date_confidence: Attested year, and a correction. The research pool called Cerf a founding board member and, elsewhere, founding chairman; both are false. ICANN's own article records incorporation in California on 30 September 1998 with Esther Dyson as founding chairwoman, and Cerf joining the board in 1999. Month and day are defaults. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Marina del Rey pin, inherited byte for byte from diffie.journey.json.
stops.campa: Cerf joins the board of the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, the body created the year before to hold the domain name system and the number registries once the United States government steps back from them. He is not, as the story is usually told, a founding director: the corporation was incorporated in California in September 1998 with Esther Dyson as founding chairwoman, and he arrives a year later to a board already seated. The two roles are not the same role.
suggested_refs: ICANN's early offices at Marina del Rey, and its 1998 incorporation under Esther Dyson
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Marina del Rey, the chair
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month: the Internet Hall of Fame gives Cerf as chairman of the ICANN board from November 2000 to November 2007. The day is a default.
stops.campa: In November Cerf becomes chairman of the ICANN board and holds the chair seven years, the whole period in which the question of who governs the internet's namespace is fought out between governments, trademark holders, and the engineers who built it. A corporation registered in California is deciding what a domain name is worth and who may sell one. The body is resented by nearly everyone who appears before it, and Cerf sits at the head of its table for all seven years.
suggested_refs: The ICANN chairmanship, November 2000 to November 2007
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography

stops.name: Reston, the internet is for everyone
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month from the document itself: RFC 3271, 'The Internet is for Everyone,' Vint Cerf, April 2002. The day is a default and the coordinate is his Virginia working base rather than a place of composition, which no source names.
stops.campa: Cerf publishes RFC 3271 in the same numbered series he has been writing in since 1969, and this one contains no state tables at all. It is an argument: that the network should reach everyone, that it should not be the privilege of the wealthy or of any single language, that governments blocking it stand against the design of the thing itself. He lists the obstacles item by item, in a document type reserved for protocol specifications. The closing line is an exhortation and not a specification.
stops.quote: Internet IS for everyone - but it won't be unless WE make it so.
stops.quote_source: RFC 3271, 'The Internet is for Everyone,' Vint Cerf, April 2002, closing line
suggested_refs: RFC 3271, the argument rather than the specification

stops.name: San Francisco, the Turing Award
stops.date_confidence: Attested award and year of citation, reconstructed ceremony. The ACM gave Cerf and Kahn the 2004 A. M. Turing Award; the research pool declines to confirm the ceremony's city or venue, and the banquet moves among cities year by year. Month and day are defaults. The coordinate is the atlas's San Francisco pin, used in phil_zimmermann.journey.json for the EFF Pioneer Award, and stands for the award lineage rather than for a confirmed hall.
stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery gives Cerf and Kahn the A. M. Turing Award for the design and implementation of the internet's basic protocols. The prize carries the name of a man who never saw a network. Ten years on, the same award goes to Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman for the other half of the problem, which is not how strangers reach each other but how they speak once they have. The pin is the San Francisco coordinate where Phil Zimmermann took the Pioneer Award from a list already carrying Cerf's name.

stops.name: Mountain View, the title he invents for himself
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month: Wikipedia has Cerf working for Google as a vice president and Chief Internet Evangelist from October 2005. The day is a default. The Googleplex pin is reconstruction as to any particular visit; his working office was the company's Reston building, and the research pool confirms no dated appearance in Mountain View.
stops.campa: Cerf leaves MCI for Google in October and takes the title Chief Internet Evangelist, which he more or less invents to describe what he means to do. He is sixty two, and the largest single company on the network hires the man who wrote the network's protocol to explain it in public and to argue for keeping it open. He works mostly from the company's Reston office, in the same Virginia corridor as DARPA and MCI and CNRI before it, and comes west for the things that need a body in Mountain View.
suggested_refs: The office of Chief Internet Evangelist, a title with one holder

stops.name: The White House, the Presidential Medal of Freedom
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: White House press records of the Presidential Medal of Freedom ceremony of 9 November 2005, at which President George W. Bush honored Cerf and Kahn. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical White House pin, shared with george_w_bush.journey.json.
stops.campa: President George W. Bush gives Cerf and Kahn the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor the country has, for the design of the internet's basic architecture. It is the same building in which they stood eight years earlier for a lesser medal for the same invention. Cerf receives it in the three piece suit and pocket square he has worn to every public occasion for decades, dressed like a banker among engineers, which is by now the one thing about him recognizable on sight.

stops.name: The United States Capitol, the argument for neutrality
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the date. The research pool carries the February 2006 network neutrality testimony at reconstruction, citing Senate Commerce Committee hearing records and press coverage without a confirmed day; the hearing records themselves were not opened. Day is a default and the coordinate is the Capitol rather than a named hearing room.
stops.campa: Cerf testifies to the Senate on network neutrality, arguing as the architect of the thing that its founding property, that any application may run on it without a carrier's permission, is now for sale. Telephone companies want to charge for priority. He spent the 1970s making dissimilar networks behave as one network; he spends this morning arguing against letting the one network be sorted back into tiers by whoever owns the wire underneath it. The gateway he named in 1974 is defined as a machine that does not know what it is carrying, and so cannot charge more for some of it.
stops.quote: How easy to say - how hard to achieve!
stops.quote_source: RFC 3271, 'The Internet is for Everyone,' Vint Cerf, April 2002, opening line
suggested_refs: Senate Commerce Committee hearings on network neutrality, February 2006

What these two made is a set of rules for behavior between machines owned by people who have never met. The ceremonies of this period are held in the Akron area, before the institution moves its museum to Alexandria; the hall used for this induction is not confirmed anywhere consulted.

segments.name: The Long Chairmanship, and the Canon

stops.name: Marina del Rey, the chairmanship ends
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month: the Internet Hall of Fame closes Cerf's ICANN chairmanship in November 2007. The day is a default. Diffie's ICANN post of May 2010 to October 2012 is carried in diffie.journey.json, whose coordinate this stop shares byte for byte.
stops.campa: Cerf steps down from the ICANN chair in November after seven years, leaving the namespace to its next quarrel. Whitfield Diffie will take a senior security post in this same institution in 2010 and leave it in 2012, the only governance office of his own working life. The two men who between them wrote how machines find one another and how they keep a secret both end up, a decade apart, in the front office of an address book in a Los Angeles marina.
suggested_refs: ICANN's Marina del Rey years, held in turn by Cerf and by Diffie

stops.name: Geneva, the Internet Hall of Fame
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day, with an unresolved coordinate contradiction. Wikipedia's 'Internet Hall of Fame' has thirty-three inaugural inductees announced on 23 April 2012 at the Internet Society's Global INET conference in Geneva, Cerf among the Pioneers. No source consulted names Palexpo as the venue, though the research pool's geography lens labelled it so and pinned 46.2381, 6.1092 while its afterlife lens pinned central Geneva; the central pair is used and the disagreement is recorded.
stops.campa: The Internet Society names its first Hall of Fame class at the Global INET conference in Geneva, thirty three people, and Cerf is among the Pioneers. The category is for work predating the commercial internet entirely. Geneva formally canonizes a history lived almost wholly in Californian and Virginian offices. He is sixty eight and has been receiving the honors of this history for fifteen years; the sources name the city and the conference but not the building, so the pin is the city and no more.

stops.name: London, the Queen Elizabeth Prize
stops.date_confidence: Attested year and ceremony: Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering award records give the 2013 prize to Cerf with Kahn and other internet pioneers, presented at Buckingham Palace. Month is from the research pool and the day is a default.
stops.campa: Cerf and Kahn receive the Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering with the other pioneers named in the citation, a prize founded two years earlier to be engineering's equivalent of a Nobel and awarded now for the first time, in a ceremony at Buckingham Palace. Several men are named for one machine that has no owner. Forty years after a sketch made in a hotel lobby outside Palo Alto, the sketch is honored in a room built centuries before anybody had a word for a packet.

stops.name: San Jose, the digital dark age
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month: Cerf's digital dark age warning was made in remarks to the AAAS meeting of February 2015 and carried widely in the press. The day is a default and the coordinate is the meeting city.
stops.campa: Cerf warns a scientific meeting in San Jose of a digital dark age: that the formats and the software of this century will become unreadable, that a family's photographs and a nation's records alike may survive as bit patterns nobody can open. The man who spent a working life making certain a message arrives now says arrival is not the whole of the problem, and that a century of ordinary life may prove less legible to its descendants than a clay tablet is to us.
suggested_refs: Cerf's AAAS remarks of February 2015 on format obsolescence
sources: AAAS conference remarks, February 2015, and subsequent press coverage

stops.name: Houston, the protocol above the atmosphere
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month: Wikipedia dates the installation of delay-tolerant networking aboard the International Space Station to June 2016. The day is a default. The station has no fixed terrestrial coordinate, so the pin is the mission control that operates it and stands below the thing it marks; the quote is from 2023 and is placed here for its subject.
stops.campa: Delay tolerant networking, the protocol family Cerf began at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in 1998, is installed aboard the International Space Station and operated from the ground. Packets are held rather than dropped when the far end is behind a planet or below a horizon. The station itself has no fixed coordinate on any map, so this pin is the mission control that flies it, and the honest statement is that the network in question passes above the pin rather than through it.
stops.quote: I'm not going to see the end of this. I feel like I'm in chapter two of what will be a much longer story about the history of interplanetary networking.
stops.quote_source: Vint Cerf, quoted in Tekla S. Perry, 'Meet Mr. Internet: Vint Cerf,' IEEE Spectrum, 30 April 2023
suggested_refs: Delay-tolerant networking aboard the International Space Station, June 2016

stops.name: Sacramento, the late honors
stops.date_confidence: Attested years, defaulted month and day, unlocated ceremonies. Wikipedia's awards list gives the IEEE Medal of Honor in 2023 and induction into the California Hall of Fame in 2024; the research pool gives no venue for the 2023 medal beyond USA, and the Sacramento coordinate stands for the state's own hall.
stops.campa: California puts Cerf in its Hall of Fame in 2024, a year after the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers gives him its Medal of Honor, the oldest and highest award it has. He is eighty one. The Valley boy who wrote statistics software for rocket engines is entered on his state's list of its own, and the honors have long since stopped marking anything he did recently and begun marking that he is still here to receive them. No venue for the 2023 medal is recorded in the sources consulted.
stops.quote: There are some people who imagine that older adults don't know how to use the internet. My immediate reaction is, 'I've got news for you, we invented it.'
stops.quote_source: Vint Cerf, interviewed by David Frank, AARP Bulletin, vol. 57 no. 10, December 2016, p. 30
suggested_refs: The IEEE Medal of Honor, 2023, and the California Hall of Fame, 2024

stops.name: Reston, the title closes
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month and a correction to the research pool, which wrote the Google tenure as ongoing in three separate entries. Wikipedia reads: Cerf worked for Google as a vice president and Chief Internet Evangelist from October 2005 to July 2026. The day is a default. The coordinate sits within about 100 m of Google's Reston office at 1875 Explorer Street.
stops.campa: In July 2026 Cerf's twenty one years as Google's Chief Internet Evangelist come to an end. He is eighty three and alive as this is written, which makes him unusual in this atlas: there is no tomb to describe, no monument, no statue, and no posthumous quarrel over what he meant. What stands in place of a grave is a numbered series of documents anyone may read, and a protocol running on every continent and above them. He is still arguing that it should belong to everyone.
suggested_refs: Google's Reston office at 1875 Explorer Street, the evangelist's working address
